snippet: Rep. Keven Stratton, R-Orem, the House sponsor of the Utah bill, cited Condic's testimony in his defense of the law. 'We all need to recognize that our understanding of medicine and human life is evolving,' Stratton said. 'And as that evolves, let's create a safe harbor for a fetus 20 weeks and older.' Stratton said the bill was not drafted with a specific procedure in mind. 'We've been told by the medical profession that there's many different options,' Stratton said. 'I would leave that up to the doctor and the patient.'

HB 467 delicenses abortion clinics in Utah and requires abortions be performed in hospitals or hospital clinics, restricts abortion exceptions in the trigger ban to apply only where the pregnant person is experiencing a life-threatening physical condition, and restricts abortion access for survivors of rape or incest to before 18 weeks gestation, among other changes to Utah's abortion laws. Keven J. Stratton appears in the House roll call votes section, where he voted Yes on the bill's passage.

Prevents an abortion clinic from being licensed after May 2, 2023, and from operating on or after January 1, 2024. The measure passed on March 3, 2023. Yes: 56 | No: 14 | None: 5 | Total: 75. Keven J. Stratton voted Yes on HB467.

Keven J. Stratton (District 48) was among 80 Utah state legislators who signed an amicus brief urging the Supreme Court to uphold the state's same-sex marriage ban. The brief argued that permitting same-sex marriage would logically lead to acceptance of polygamous and incestuous unions. The lawmakers stated: 'If the choice of marriage partners is an unlimited fundamental right... then the fundamental rights analysis applied by the Tenth Circuit will apply with even greater force to consenting adults desiring polygamous marriage.'

Republican Sen. Keven Stratton sponsored Senate Bill 174, which would permit healthcare providers to decline treatments conflicting with their religious or moral convictions. Providers would need to notify the Utah Department of Health and Human Services and post office notices about their objections. Emergency care would be exempt from these provisions. Stratton stated: 'Just want to assure that the thing that this bill does is we talk about procedures and not people. The idea is we treat all human beings equally in this bill.' He explained that current protections exist in federal law rather than state law, and enforcement can shift depending on which administration is in office.

Sen. Keven Stratton, R-Orem, co-sponsored resolution HCR15 with Rep. Michael Petersen, which they describe as encouraging 'practices that exemplify religious freedom in public spaces.' Stratton stated: 'When you take God out of society, you create a vacuum, and it's going to be filled. To invite that Judeo-Christian value back into the public square allows all sorts of the things many of us were yearning for to heal the wounds of our nation and bring us together as a people.' On inclusive intent: 'It's trying to invite people of all faiths to be respected and allowed in the discussions — all faiths or no faiths — to truly be free exercise.'

Senator Keven Stratton (R-Orem) sponsored SB193, which would designate Good Friday as an official state holiday in Utah. He described this as 'the second of a two-session effort to recognize the great religious diversity that we have here in the state.' Stratton emphasized that supporting Good Friday recognition connects to his broader commitment to religious freedom. He stated: 'Religious liberty is the taproot of all our freedoms and as we honor that we really strengthen our society.'

Starting in 2029, voters will have to opt-in every eight years to receive mail ballots, rather than automatically receiving them. The bill also requires voters to add the last four digits of valid identification on the ballot along with their signature starting in 2026. A signature will no longer be required in 2029. The Senate voted 19-10 to approve the bill, mostly along party lines. The measure was signed by Gov. Spencer Cox.

In the last legislative session, we unanimously passed and Gov. Spencer Cox signed HCR1, 'Concurrent Resolution to Work Together to Address the Climate, Public Lands, and Carbon Sequestration,' which lays out a win-win strategy for protecting and improving our natural resources and the environment while also significantly controlling greenhouse gases. The underlying approach in HCR1 is to protect the atmospheric carbon now being stored in natural systems like forests and rangeland soils while also sequestering additional CO2 by better harnessing the processes nature has perfected and proven throughout the ages. Applying this test would allow us to transition to the energy sources of the future more gradually, rationally, economically and responsibly while still addressing climate concerns. — authored by Keven Stratton.
